column5: The newspapers carry this information often.
column8: This is a difficult incentive issue. Institutional context differs across countries and is important.
column11: There are a number of qualifications, such as it depends on the current price, but in general one important problem is the low prices.
It has clearly been a failure, but I can't claim to know what exactly went wrong.

column5: Supply curves slope up...  (but it does not necessarily mean that EU chose the wrong price. it may, it may not)
column8: again, holds as a matter of logic...  if you want to affect production, subsidize production.  Otherwise, money may leak elsewhere.
column11: I do not know what the right price is...

column5: Firms respond to markets - higher prices would increase vaccine supply.
column8: Paying more for vaccines is a clear way to boost supply. It also supports R&D for vaccines for future pandemics.
column11: The benefit of a vaccine far outweighs the costs, so paying more for vaccines makes long-run economic sense.
But it would be at the expense of someone else - not sure there would be any gain overall!

column5: Offering higher prices would have led to higher profits of pharma companies. Monopolists do not increase supply with higher prices.
column11: What the EU and other countries should have done is to revoke patent rights. That would have boosted the supply

column5: The time required to increase capacity may be too long for the price increase to have a significant impact

column11: It is unclear how much this would help now in speeding up vaccine productions, but it would have helped in the past.

column8: The question is not clear. How would "paying for capacity" be structured? Would "higher prices" increase quantity guarantees?
column11: Even if lockdowns cost "only" 2% GDP per year, accelerating vaccination by half a year would save EU 300 euros per capita.

column5: I suspect that unit price not the only — or even the main — dimension of the contract negotiations resulting now in slow deliveries.
column8: Not clear that price and quantity deal any worse than pay for capacity deal given creditworthiness of EU buyers.
column11: Capacity is the problem now. Vaccine is clearly worth more than €100, but paying this to divert a small amount from ROW seems bad diplomacy.

column8: It may not be possible to expand capacity at a short notice.

column5: It is as simple as that. Note that equity-like co-investments in such facilities would have been even better, overcoming risk aversion.
column8: Both should work together. Ultimately, fast inventors have to benefit.
column11: The higher price goes into the right direction - ultimately different cost and benefit effects have to be aggregated.

column8: Answer depends on what the bottle neck is. If it is capacity, then cap. subsidies help. If it is inputs, then higher prices likely better.
column11: It's fairly clear that "value"/dose to EU is well above current prices but don't know if raising now would help much. Should've done earlier

column8: Uncertainty over demand means that pharma companies do not invest early enough in capacity: paying for capacity is one way to address that
column11: I just don't know the cost (and benefit) figures well enough to answer this one
Paying higher prices might not guarantee substantially more vaccines now.

column8: Investments in vaccines are sunk cost. Higher prices NOW would only reallocate doses to EU from others. But larger production would help all

column11: I'd agree if there were no diversion from rest of world but that seems a major issue

column5: All inputs are man-made; offering "zero profit" and high liabilities cannot result in best-of-class investments...
column8: more unclear; ultimately, what matters is shots in arms; capacity is easier to game

column5: I don't know enough to answer. I would guess the financial incentives were strong enough even at the prices the EU negotiated.
column8: Seems like a more direct way to deal with the shortage of supply.
column11: If payment at this level could lead to taking many months off lockdown, then it likely pays for itself.

column5: We don't know the prices paid but that seems to have been the successful strategy of Israel.
column11: Cost-benefits calculations are imprecise and pricing human life is dicy. But the costs of lockdowns alone probably easily pass the bar.
